name: Dorik
tagline: Build a small responsive site with pages, collections, and simple forms
verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Dorik, build a small responsive site with pages, collections, and simple forms. The hard boundary is hosting, cms, memberships, templates, and no-code editing polish, plus editor polish, hosting, templates, and ecosystem.
coreLoopDIY: Assemble a small responsive site from sections with pages, collections, and simple forms, edit copy and media, preview breakpoints, and publish a static site to a user-owned target.
whatYouLose: hosting, CMS, memberships, templates, and no-code editing polish
moatType: editor polish, hosting, templates, and ecosystem
ongoingBurden: responsive rendering, forms, domains, certificates, deploys, backups, template maintenance, and browser regressions
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Dorik because the page renderer is reproducible, but customers pay to avoid becoming their own hosting and browser-compatibility team. The recurring cost buys responsive rendering, forms, domains, certificates, deploys, backups, template maintenance, and browser regressions, not just the visible interface.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Personal plan and a single-site builder DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Dorik in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and static export; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: assemble a small responsive site from sections with pages, collections, and simple forms, edit copy and media, preview breakpoints, and publish a static site to a user-owned target.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Provide a section library for hero, proof, features, pricing, FAQ, and footer blocks.
Use a constrained design-token system rather than arbitrary CSS controls.
Allow inline text editing and local image upload with responsive optimization.
Preview desktop, tablet, and mobile widths and surface overflow errors.
Persist projects in SQLite and support a portable JSON export.
Generate a clean static Next.js output and document deployment to one target.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a plugin marketplace.
Deliberately leave out multi-tenant managed hosting.
Deliberately leave out advanced ecommerce, memberships, and agency billing.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
